title: What is the Young Generation, how does Minor GC work (copying collection, Eden to Survivor, aging, tenuring threshold 15), and why is copying collection fragmentation-free?
shortTitle: How does Minor GC work in the Young Generation?

s1_definition.profdef: The Young generation is the part of the heap where newly created objects are first allocated. It is divided into Eden, where objects are born, and two equal Survivor spaces, S0 and S1. A Minor garbage collection runs when Eden fills; it is a copying collection that finds the live objects in Eden and the in-use Survivor space, copies them into the other Survivor space while incrementing each object's age, and then declares the vacated regions entirely empty. Objects that survive enough minor collections, by default up to a tenuring threshold of fifteen, are promoted to the Old generation. Copying collection is fragmentation-free because it compacts the survivors together as it copies them, leaving a single contiguous free area.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Eden as the busy new-accounts counter at National Bank of India where every new folder starts. When the counter gets full, a quick sweep (Minor GC) happens: a clerk takes only the folders still in use and neatly moves them to a clean holding shelf (a Survivor space), stamping each with a tally mark for how many sweeps it has survived, and then wipes the whole counter clean in one motion. Folders that keep getting used and collect fifteen tally marks are moved to long-term archival storage (the Old generation). Because the clerk packs the surviving folders tightly on the clean shelf, there are never awkward gaps left between them.
s1_definition.oneliner: The Young generation is Eden plus two Survivor spaces where new objects live; Minor GC copies the few survivors from Eden and one Survivor into the other, ages them, promotes long-lived ones after about fifteen rounds, and leaves no fragmentation because copying compacts as it goes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Young generation is the part of the heap where newly created objects are first allocated. It is divided into Eden, where objects are born, and two equal Survivor spaces, S0 and S1. A Minor garbage collection runs when Eden fills; it is a copying collection that finds the live objects in Eden and the in-use Survivor space, copies them into the other Survivor space while incrementing each object's age, and then declares the vacated regions entirely empty. Objects that survive enough minor collections, by default up to a tenuring threshold of fifteen, are promoted to the Old generation. Copying collection is fragmentation-free because it compacts the survivors together as it copies them, leaving a single contiguous free area.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Eden as the busy new-accounts counter at National Bank of India where every new folder starts. When the counter gets full, a quick sweep (Minor GC) happens: a clerk takes only the folders still in use and neatly moves them to a clean holding shelf (a Survivor space), stamping each with a tally mark for how many sweeps it has survived, and then wipes the whole counter clean in one motion. Folders that keep getting used and collect fifteen tally marks are moved to long-term archival storage (the Old generation). Because the clerk packs the surviving folders tightly on the clean shelf, there are never awkward gaps left between them.

**One line to remember:** The Young generation is Eden plus two Survivor spaces where new objects live; Minor GC copies the few survivors from Eden and one Survivor into the other, ages them, promotes long-lived ones after about fifteen rounds, and leaves no fragmentation because copying compacts as it goes.

sections.s2_technical:
Almost all objects are born in Eden, which is the large first section of the Young generation. The two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1, are smaller and equal in size, and at any moment one of them is empty while the other may hold previous survivors. This layout exists because of a well-known observation called the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. A banking request creates many short-lived objects, like temporary request and response wrappers, that become garbage almost immediately, so it pays to collect the young area often and cheaply.

A Minor GC triggers when Eden fills up with new allocations. The collector identifies the live objects, meaning those reachable from garbage-collection roots, in Eden and in the currently occupied Survivor space. It then copies all those live objects into the other, empty Survivor space, packing them together. Each copied object has its age counter incremented, because it has now survived one more collection. After the copy, Eden and the previously occupied Survivor space are considered completely empty and can be reused immediately; the collector does not touch the dead objects at all, it simply abandons the whole region. This is why a Minor GC is fast: its cost is proportional to the number of live objects, not the number of dead ones, and most young objects are dead.

Aging and promotion work through the age counter. Each time an object survives a Minor GC and is copied to a Survivor space, its age goes up by one. When an object's age reaches the tenuring threshold, which defaults to a maximum of fifteen in HotSpot, it is promoted, meaning copied into the Old generation instead of a Survivor space, on the assumption that it is now long-lived. The JVM can also promote earlier if a Survivor space would overflow, through a mechanism called dynamic age adjustment. A small conceptual example: a cached exchange-rate table that lives for the whole application quickly accumulates age and gets tenured, while a per-request transfer object never survives even one Minor GC.

Copying collection is fragmentation-free precisely because it relocates and compacts the live objects into a fresh space rather than freeing individual dead objects in place. A mark-and-sweep collector that frees dead objects where they lie leaves holes between the surviving objects, and over time those holes fragment the space so that a large allocation may fail even when total free memory is sufficient. A copying collector sidesteps this entirely: after it copies the survivors packed together into the empty Survivor space, all the free memory is one contiguous block, so the next allocations are simple pointer bumps. The trade-off, and the senior nuance, is that copying needs spare room to copy into, which is why a Survivor space is kept empty and why copying is used for the young area where survivors are few; you would not want to copy a huge long-lived Old generation this way, which is why the Old generation uses mark-sweep-compact or region-based collectors like G1 instead.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer API creates a flurry of short-lived objects for every request: request wrappers, validation results, and temporary calculations. These die almost immediately. This is exactly what the Young generation and Minor GC are designed for, because collecting the young area is cheap when nearly everything there is already dead.

Problem 2 — A few objects, like a shared exchange-rate cache, live for the entire run. These should not keep getting copied between Survivor spaces forever. This is exactly what aging and the tenuring threshold handle, because after surviving enough minor collections the long-lived objects are promoted to the Old generation and stop being copied.

In the mini-project we build a transfer loop that allocates many short-lived objects (to drive Minor GC) and keeps one long-lived cache object alive (to be tenured). We read the Young-generation collector's bean to count minor collections and log the behavior, illustrating the copying and promotion flow.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/younggen/YoungGenDemo.java

# Run with GC logging and an explicit tenuring threshold so you can watch aging
java -Xms256m -Xmx256m \
     -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=15 \
     -Xlog:gc+age=trace:stdout \
     -cp out com.bank.younggen.YoungGenDemo

# You will see repeated "Pause Young" lines and age histograms for survivors
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one long-lived RateCache and two million short-lived TransferRequest objects.

Step 1: The RateCache is created and placed in Eden like any new object, holding one exchange rate. A reference to it is kept for the whole run.

Step 2: The loop begins creating TransferRequest objects in Eden. Each is used to compute a fee and then immediately becomes unreachable, so it is garbage by the next iteration.

Step 3: Eden fills after many allocations and a Minor GC fires. The collector finds the live objects, which are essentially just the RateCache and whatever request is momentarily in use, copies them into the empty Survivor space, increments their age, and then wipes Eden clean in one stroke. The millions of dead requests are never individually touched.

Step 4: This repeats many times across the loop. Each Minor GC copies the RateCache from one Survivor space to the other, raising its age each time. The dead requests are abandoned en masse, keeping each collection cheap.

Step 5: Once the RateCache's age reaches the tenuring threshold of fifteen, it is promoted into the Old generation and stops being copied on every Minor GC. At the end the demo reports how many Minor GCs occurred, confirming the young area was collected repeatedly and cheaply.

```text
[INFO] processed 2,000,000 short-lived TransferRequests
[INFO] Minor GCs during run = 37 (Eden filled repeatedly, survivors copied Eden→Survivor)
[INFO] long-lived RateCache survived all Minor GCs → tenured to Old gen
[INFO] accumulated fees = Rs.2000000.000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Young Generation
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Eden  [ new TransferRequest × millions ]       │  objects born here
  │ S0 (occupied)  [ survivors, ages ]             │
  │ S1 (empty)                                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │ Eden full → MINOR GC (copying)
        ▼
  find live (RateCache + current req)
  copy live Eden+S0 → S1, age++   (dead requests abandoned)
  wipe Eden + S0 → now empty, S1 occupied (roles swap next time)
        │ repeat ... age reaches 15 (tenuring threshold)
        ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Old Generation  [ RateCache (promoted) ]       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Fragmentation-free: survivors packed contiguously in S1,
  free space is ONE contiguous block (pointer-bump allocation).
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Young Generation & Minor GC ═══

  ┌─ Mechanics ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Eden: allocation site (TLAB bump pointer)             │
  │ S0/S1: one empty, one holds aged survivors            │
  │ Minor GC = COPYING: copy live Eden+fromS → toS, age++ │
  │ cost ∝ LIVE objects (dead ones abandoned, not freed)  │
  │ age == MaxTenuringThreshold (15) → promote to Old     │
  │ early promotion if Survivor would overflow            │
  │ fragmentation-free: compaction happens via copy       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young →
    collect Young often + cheaply, Old rarely.

  Object lifecycle (state):
    [Eden] --survive--> [Survivor age1] --..--> [Survivor age15]
       │ unreachable            │ unreachable         │ promote
       ▼                        ▼                     ▼
    reclaimed next GC        reclaimed            [Old Generation]

  Reporter contract: sum GarbageCollectorMXBean.getCollectionCount()
    for young collectors (Scavenge/ParNew/G1 Young/Copy).
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Young generation is the part of the heap where newly created objects are first allocated, and it is divided into three regions: a large Eden space where objects are born, and two smaller, equal Survivor spaces called S0 and S1, of which one is always kept empty. This layout exists because of the weak generational hypothesis, the well-established observation that most objects die young. In a banking request I create a flurry of short-lived objects, like request wrappers and temporary calculations, that become garbage almost immediately, so it pays enormously to collect the young area often and cheaply.

A Minor garbage collection fires when Eden fills with new allocations. The collector identifies the live objects, meaning the ones still reachable from garbage-collection roots, in Eden and in the currently occupied Survivor space, and it copies all of them into the empty Survivor space, packing them tightly together. Each copied object has its age counter incremented, because it has survived one more collection. The key insight is what happens next: Eden and the previously occupied Survivor space are now considered completely empty and are reused immediately, and the collector never touches the dead objects at all. That is why a Minor GC is fast, because its cost is proportional to the number of live objects, not the number of dead ones, and in the young area the overwhelming majority are dead.

Aging and promotion ride on that age counter. Every time an object survives a Minor GC and gets copied, its age goes up by one, and when its age reaches the tenuring threshold, which defaults to a maximum of fifteen in HotSpot, it is promoted into the Old generation instead of being copied to a Survivor space again, on the assumption that it is now genuinely long-lived. The JVM can also promote earlier if a Survivor space would otherwise overflow. In my example a shared exchange-rate cache quickly ages and gets tenured, while a per-request transfer object never survives even one Minor GC.

Finally, the reason copying collection is fragmentation-free is that it relocates and compacts the live objects into a fresh space rather than freeing dead objects where they lie. A mark-and-sweep that frees in place leaves holes between survivors, and over time those holes fragment memory so a large allocation can fail even when there is plenty of total free space. A copying collector avoids that completely, because after it copies the survivors packed together, all the remaining free memory is one contiguous block and the next allocations are just pointer bumps. The senior trade-off I mention is that copying needs spare room to copy into, which is exactly why a Survivor space is kept empty and why copying suits the young area where survivors are few, whereas the much larger Old generation uses mark-sweep-compact or a region-based collector like G1 instead.

---

keyPoints: Minor GC: triggered when Eden is full
Live objects in Eden + S0 copied to S1 (or vice versa)
Dead objects (unreachable) are simply discarded — no sweep needed
Survivors that reach age threshold are promoted to Old Gen
Minor GC is fast (milliseconds) because most young objects are dead
